text: Provenance is the record of where something came from and whose hands it passed through on the way to you. It is used most often about art and antiques, where a painting's provenance is the documented chain of owners running back to the artist's studio, and lately about photographs and data online. It is not quite the same as origin: provenance is the traceable trail, the thing that lets you decide whether to trust what is in front of you. Here it explains why print was distrusted at first, since a printed sheet arrived anonymous and identical to a thousand others.

Sensationalism is presenting news so as to excite or shock people rather than to inform them, leading with the goriest detail or the most alarming number because that is what makes someone stop and look. The ending -ism marks it as a habit of a whole trade, and the word is nearly always an accusation; nobody calls their own work sensationalism. In this piece it names the price of the newspaper's new business model, in which whatever gathered the biggest crowd fastest had a pull on the front page.

Indiscriminate means done without making distinctions, without picking and choosing, applied to everything alike. It rests on the older and neutral sense of discriminate, which simply meant to tell things apart; today that verb usually means treating people unfairly, a narrowing of the same root. The 1904 complaint quoted here is that writers would reach for the typewriter for absolutely everything, with no judgment about which occasions deserved the slower care of a pen.

Here lead is the soft, heavy grey metal, and it rhymes with red rather than with need. Printing type was cast from it because it melts at a low temperature, flows into fine detail and is soft enough to trim, which is why the article speaks of lead letters and of a molten soup of lead, antimony and tin. Watch out for the other lead in this same article, in the bracketed phrase may lead to, which is the ordinary verb meaning to result in.

A printing press is the machine that squeezes inked type against paper, and that is the sense meant when Gutenberg invents the press or when steam-powered presses churn out books. Because newspapers were made on them, the press also came to mean the news business as a whole, the sense you hear in freedom of the press or a press conference. The article slides between the machine and the industry, which is part of its point: the machine is what made the industry possible.

In printing, to compose means to set type, assembling a page letter by letter, and a person who does it is a compositor. So composing by hand here has nothing to do with writing music or writing an essay; it is the physical work of picking metal blocks out of a case and packing them into lines. That is why the rival machine in the article is called the Paige Compositor.

Type means the metal blocks that carry the raised letters a press prints from, so setting type, lines of type and Hot Type all point at that physical stuff. The word then spread to the shapes of the letters themselves, which is where typeface and typography come from. Confusingly, the article also uses type in its everyday sense once, when paper of wood pulp is called cheaper than the old type made of rags, where it just means kind.

Practically here means almost or very nearly, not in a practical manner. So the Linotype being in use in practically all large newspapers means nearly every one of them, with a handful of exceptions. English keeps a few adverbs like this that quietly mean almost, including virtually and all but.

To cultivate literally means to prepare and tend soil so a crop will grow, and the figurative use keeps the sense of patient, deliberate growing over time. Cultivating an air of objectivity means the newspapers worked at building that reputation on purpose, tending it, rather than simply having it. The same figurative move gives us cultivating a friendship or cultivating a taste for something.

Literally to illuminate is to light something up, and the figurative sense used here is to make something clearer or easier to understand, as if a light had been shone on it. Saying a history helps illuminate the present moment means it explains today by showing where today came from. The related noun illuminating is a common compliment for a book or a lecture.

An institution is an established organisation with rules and a life of its own, one that outlasts the particular people running it, such as a court, a university or a long-lived newspaper. Calling a paper more of an institution is the opposite of calling it one owner's personal project: it means the thing had become bigger and more permanent than whoever happened to own it. The word can also describe a building, but the point being made here is about permanence and independence.

Beyond animals, a creature of someone or something means a person or body that owes its existence to them and is wholly under their control, almost their invention. Saying a newspaper was less the creature of their proprietor means it had stopped being simply the owner's instrument, doing whatever they wanted. You will meet the same construction in phrases like a creature of Congress or a creature of habit.

Scale here means sheer size or extent, not a weighing machine or a musical scale. The scale of investment required for modernisation means how enormous the sums were, and Scale led to more advertising means that the sheer size of the audience did. Business writing leans on this word constantly, as in economies of scale or scaling up, and it almost always means how big, not how heavy.

A daily is a newspaper published every day, as opposed to a weekly or a monthly, so New York alone had 46 dailies means forty-six separate daily papers competing in one city. English does this often, turning a description of how often something appears into a noun for the thing itself. The same trick gives us a weekly, a quarterly and the periodicals mentioned nearby.

A supplement is something added on to complete or extend a main thing. In publishing it means an extra section bundled into a newspaper, such as a magazine, a sports pull-out or a colour weekend section, which is what 48-pagers stuffed with supplements refers to. It is the same word as the vitamin supplements on a shelf, but here nothing is being swallowed.

A winch is a drum you crank or power to wind a rope or cable in, used to haul heavy things up. So the New York Tribune winched its first one up to its ninth-floor office means the machine was hoisted up the outside of the building on a cable, because a Linotype weighed on the order of a ton and would never have gone up a staircase. The detail is there to make you feel how enormous these machines were.

Latter means the later of two, or the second of two things just mentioned, and its partner word is former. The latter half of the 19th century therefore means roughly 1850 to 1900, the second of the century's two halves. Keep it apart from later, which simply means further on in time.

Objectivity is the practice of reporting what happened without letting your own side, interests or feelings shape it, so that a reader on either side would accept the account. It is treated as a professional ideal in journalism and in science, and it is famously hard to reach completely. The article is careful to say newspapers cultivated at least an air of objectivity, which hints that the appearance of it was commercially useful whether or not the reality followed.

Bloomers were loose, gathered underpants worn by women and girls in the 19th century, named after the American campaigner Amelia Bloomer. They matter to this sentence because paper used to be made from pulped cotton and linen rags, so worn-out underwear was raw material for the paper industry, valuable enough that some governments banned its export. It is a real fact dressed up as a joke.

To do something on the fly is to do it while everything is still moving, without stopping to set up first. Moulding whole lines of type on the fly means the metal was cast line by line as the operator kept typing, rather than being prepared in advance. The phrase is now everywhere in ordinary speech, as in changing the plan on the fly.

When something catches on, it becomes popular and spreads. Edison's electric pen did not catch on, meaning people simply did not take it up. The same phrasal verb has a second common meaning, to finally understand something, as in it took him a while to catch on.

To turn out something, in this sense, is to produce it, especially in quantity and by machine, the way a factory turns out cars. So You can't turn out thought by machinery is a claim that thinking is not the kind of thing a machine can manufacture. Do not confuse it with the other common turn out, meaning to prove to be the case.

To churn out something is to produce it steadily and in large quantities, often with a hint that quality suffers for the speed. Steam-powered presses churned out books and newspapers gives you the sense of an endless mechanical flow. The image comes from a butter churn, worked round and round without stopping.

If something is under way it has already begun and is in progress. A news revolution was under way means the change had started, not that it was about to. The phrase comes from sailing, where a ship under way has got moving through the water.

In today's terms means converted into modern money, so that an old sum can be compared with prices now. Twain invested millions in today's terms, meaning that whatever the original figure was, it would buy millions of dollars' worth today. Journalists add this because inflation makes historical amounts meaningless on their own.

An air of something is the appearance or impression of it, the manner a person or thing gives off. Cultivating at least an air of objectivity is a delicately worded way of saying the newspapers looked even-handed, without promising they truly were. The phrase almost always carries that faint suggestion of surface over substance.

The Linotype was a typesetting machine, introduced in the 1880s, that cast a whole line of type in one piece of hot metal as the operator typed at a keyboard, instead of a person placing single letters by hand. Its name comes from that idea, a line of type. For most of the 20th century it set the type for the majority of the world's books and newspapers.

Ottmar Mergenthaler was the German-born American inventor of the Linotype, who arrived in Baltimore in 1872 with almost nothing and had trained as a watchmaker rather than a printer. The article suggests his ignorance of printing helped, because he was not attached to the existing way of doing the job. He died in 1899 at 45, but his machine stayed in service for about a century.

Johannes Gutenberg was the German goldsmith who, around 1450, brought movable metal type together with a screw press to make printing practical in Europe. He is the reference point of the whole article: the striking claim is that four centuries later, type was still being set by hand more or less as he had done it. Everything else about publishing had changed; that one step had not.

Typesetting is the job of building a page out of individual pieces of metal type before it can be printed, letter by letter and line by line, with blank spacers wedged in to make the lines even. A person who did it was a typesetter or compositor, and it was skilled, slow, expensive work. Mechanising it is the whole subject of this article.

A matrix, plural matrices, is a mould: a small brass block with a letter shape sunk into it, so that molten metal poured in comes out as a raised letter ready to print. The Linotype held a magazine of these, and pressing a key released the matrix for that letter into place. So the operator was not handling letters at all, only the moulds the letters would be cast from.

Antimony is a brittle, silvery chemical element mixed into the lead used for printing type. It is there for a physical reason worth knowing: most metals shrink as they cool, but an alloy with antimony expands slightly, so the cast letter fills the mould completely and comes out sharp. Printers' type metal was typically lead with antimony and a little tin for toughness.

The Paige Compositor was the Linotype's great rival, a machine that tried to mechanise the handling of individual metal letters rather than bypass it. With more than 18,000 parts it was fantastically complicated and kept breaking down, and it lost. Mark Twain's investment in it is the reason he is in this story at all.

Mark Twain was the American writer of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn, and he began his working life as a typesetter, which is why this machine fascinated him. He poured what would be millions in today's money into the losing Paige Compositor, and that helped bankrupt him. His verdict on it, a monument of human ingenuity and stupidity, is quoted here.

Thomas Edison was the American inventor behind the phonograph and a practical electric light, and the holder of over a thousand patents. He appears here for a failure rather than a success: his electric pen for cutting stencils did not catch on. The detail the article enjoys is that its mechanism was adapted into the first electric tattoo needle.

Rupert Murdoch is the Australian-born media owner whose newspapers include the Sun and the Times in Britain and the Wall Street Journal in America. The 1986 revolution referred to here is his move of London newspaper production to Wapping, which replaced hot-metal typesetting with computers and broke the print unions after a long and bitter strike. It is the moment the Linotype era actually ended in Britain.

The telegraph sent messages as pulses of electric current along a wire, tapped out in code and written down at the far end, so news could cross a country in minutes instead of travelling at the speed of a horse or a ship. It is the first technology in the article's list because it separated the movement of information from the movement of people. Newspapers were its first great customer.

Periodicals are publications that come out at regular intervals, which covers magazines, journals and newspapers alike. The word is useful precisely because it is broad, so counting newspapers and periodicals together captures the whole printed press. Its root is period, meaning a repeating stretch of time.

Mass media means channels that deliver the same content to an enormous, undifferentiated audience at once, such as newspapers, radio, film and television. The idea is in the word mass: not a message to a person or a village, but one message to millions of strangers simultaneously. The article's argument is that this became possible only when typesetting stopped being a handmade bottleneck.

A trade union is an organisation of workers who bargain with their employer together rather than one by one, which gives them far more leverage, and whose main weapon is the strike. The print unions in Britain were unusually powerful because stopping a handful of skilled typesetters stopped the entire newspaper that night. That is why they could keep an obsolete machine in use for years after better technology existed.

A contraption is a machine or device, described with a touch of amusement as if it were oddly made, overcomplicated or slightly ridiculous. Calling the Linotype a forgotten contraption is affectionate rather than dismissive, and it fits a machine full of clattering levers and molten metal. A neutral writer would have said device or machine.

Pallid means pale, especially unhealthily or unusually so, drained of colour. Short and pallid with ginger whiskers is a quick physical sketch of Mergenthaler as unimpressive to look at, which sets up the surprise of what he achieved. The word can also describe something feeble or lacking force, as in a pallid performance.

Fiddly describes something awkward to handle because the parts are small and need delicate finger work, like threading a needle or the clasp on a bracelet. The fiddly letters means the tiny metal blocks a typesetter had to pick up and place one at a time. It is a common British word and it quietly explains why the job was so slow.

To perforate something is to pierce it with a hole or a row of holes. Edison's electric pen used a rapidly vibrating needle to perforate paper, turning a drawing into a pattern of tiny holes. You meet the same root in the perforated line on a sheet of stamps, made to tear neatly.

A stencil is a sheet with shapes cut out of it, so that ink or paint pushed through the gaps reproduces those shapes on whatever lies underneath. Edison's pen made stencils by punching holes along the lines of your writing, and ink rolled over the sheet then came through as a copy. It was a way of duplicating a document before photocopiers existed.

Of a person, temperamental means moody and easily upset; of a machine, it means unreliable and liable to work beautifully one moment and not at all the next. The Paige was delicate and temperamental uses the second sense, and the 18,000 parts explain why. It is one of those words we lend to machines as if they had moods.

Ingenuity is cleverness at inventing things and solving practical problems, the quality of a good engineer or a resourceful improviser. Twain's line about a monument of human ingenuity and stupidity works by yoking it to its opposite: the Paige Compositor was brilliantly clever and completely misguided at the same time. The related adjective is ingenious.

A proprietor is an owner, especially of a business, and in this context the individual owner of a newspaper. The point of the phrase less the creature of their proprietor is that once papers required huge investment, they grew too large for any one owner's personality to run through everything they printed. Newspaper proprietor is still the standard term in British writing for a press baron.
